# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–19 (Complete – Updated 139)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of fifth year** (Chapter 19). Summer 1816: Sir Pitt (elder) dies; Pitt becomes Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet, MP. Spring 1816: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor); Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house; Lady Southdown assumes control; Miss Crawley dies. **Chapter 18 events (Summer 1816)**: Sir Pitt nearly eighty, afflicted with lumbago; Pitt and Lady Jane visit Queen's Crawley. Sir Pitt collapses after heavy drinking, dies during summer. **Chapter 18-19 transition**: Within three-to-four days of inheriting, Pitt determines to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations. **Chapter 19 (Autumn, fifth year)**: Briggs dismissed by Lady Southdown; Miss Crawley's legacies distributed; Bowls and Firkin receive legacies, marry, set up lodging-house in London. Rawdon and Rebecca visit Queen's Crawley for Sir Pitt's funeral ceremonies (the text describes it as autumn, with gravel walk and terrace scraped clean, grand hatchment over entrance, multiple mourners assembled).
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' Coffee-house, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera, Knightsbridge, nursery, parlour, ring, Times Office in City, Piccadilly, Bowls's lodging-house), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calais, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, Miremere, Valenciennes, Kensington Gardens, Hampshire, Madras, district chapel, tavern, Winchester Cathedral Close, Mudbury, Rectory, Parsonage, Hill farms of Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Southampton Gaol, Dunwick, Crawley Arms, Mudbury (saddler residence), Salwick harbour town, parsonage with lavender.

## Main Characters

**Sir Pitt Crawley (Baronet, elder) – DECEASED (Summer 1816)**
- Nearly eighty; afflicted with lumbago. **Final days and death (Chapter 18)**: Collapsed after heavy rum-and-water drinking; conducted to bedroom; could not speak but recognized people. After seventy years of cunning, struggling, drinking, scheming, sin and selfishness, became "whimpering old idiot put in and out of bed and cleaned and fed like a baby." Died summer 1816; all blinds pulled down; church bell tolled; chancel hung in black. Funeral ceremonies held at Queen's Crawley in autumn, requiring many persons in black assembled at place, including household staff, alms house women, parish officials, undertaker's men.

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Now Baronet, MP (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Upon father's death**: Immediately plans to clear estate with ready money. Within three-to-four days, bearing changed; fixes plans to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, be friendliest terms with blood relations. Pleased to think he should be chief; proposes to use vast influence for county position to place brother Rawdon and provide decently for cousins. Called Lady Southdown "Lady Macbeth"; when she waited for weakness, rose scared and left library. Told her she won't go away; she let house at Brighton, spent dividends; impossible two chiefs in family. **Chapter 19 (Funeral occasion)**: In black, ready to receive returning brother and wife. Heightened colour; shook Rawdon by hand; saluted Rebecca with handshake and low bow. Judged correctly Lady Southdown would not quit premises; she preserves solemn stony silence in company of Pitt and rebellious wife; frightens children in nursery with ghastly gloom. Only faint head-dress bending welcomed Rawdon and Rebecca. **Pitt's bearing**: Has gotten fat; doing the thing handsomely (per Rawdon's assessment).

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Upon Pitt's letter (Chapter 18)**: But half-pleased; thought "What's use of going down to stupid place?"; horses there and back cost twenty pounds. **Wife's ambitions (Chapter 18)**: Rebecca tells him she means for him to get Parliament seat, for herself Court presentation, for him place through Lord Steyne's influence (Irish Secretary, West Indian Governor, Treasurer, Consul, or such). **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: Turned red passing through old hall with Rebecca, arm in arm. Abashed and cast down; recollections of boyhood, innocence, Eton, mother (frigid demure woman), sister he was passionately fond of (now dead), how he used to thrash Pitt, little Rawdy at home. Encouraged by Lady Jane's affection toward Rebecca, twirled mustachios and saluted Lady Jane with kiss, causing her to blush exceedingly. **Verdict afterward**: "Dev'lish nice little woman, Lady Jane." Agreed with Rebecca that mother-in-law was "tremendous old Guy" and sisters "rather well-looking young women."

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley) (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Character and social position (Chapter 18)**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; displays herself at gatherings; sings charming French songs, plays piano, charms with wit. Manipulates husband through derision of paternal tenderness; instructs him to spread news of inheritance; controls him through scorn. **Toward Briggs (Chapter 19)**: Recognizes fatigued Briggs on street; pulls up carriage and ponies; embraces warmly; they retire to Mrs. Bowls's front parlour with red moreen curtains and round looking-glass with chained eagle. Briggs cried; Becky laughed and kissed her. Rebecca gave narrative of own life with usual artlessness and candour. **Benevolent plans (Chapter 19)**: Upon finding Briggs has Miss Crawley's legacy and needs no salary, instantly forms domestic plans. Invites Briggs to dinner to see "dear little darling Rawdon." Within one week Briggs comes to live with her; within six months Briggs has lent Rawdon Crawley six hundred pounds upon annuity. Mrs. Bowls cautioned Briggs against "lion's den" warning. **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: Somewhat pale passing through old hall; pinched husband's arm entering oak parlour. Rebecca felt faint bending of head-dress and plumes from Lady Southdown. **Emotional response**: Lady Jane's embrace brought tears into eyes of "little adventuress"—which ornaments, as narrator notes, "she wore very seldom." Artless mark of kindness and confidence touched and pleased her. **Afterward**: Agreed with Rawdon that Pitt got fat and doing thing handsomely; "he can afford it." **Toward sisters-in-law (Chapter 19)**: Did not attempt to forget former position of Governess; recalled it frankly and kindly; asked them about studies with great gravity; told them she had thought of them many days and longed to know of their welfare. Made it appear she had not ceased keeping them uppermost in her thoughts and taking tenderest interest in their welfare since leaving them. **Bowing and recognizing (Chapter 19)**: In park with half-dozen dandies cantering after carriage; whirled away into Piccadilly nodding with sweetest smiles; these recognitions were inexpressibly pleasant to her; seemed as if she was not an imposter anymore and was coming to home of her ancestors.

**Little Rawdon (Son) (Chapter 18-19)**
- **London period (Chapter 18)**: Hidden upstairs in garret or kitchen, scarcely noticed by mother; passed days with French bonne; when Frenchwoman departed, taken to housemaid's bed in garret by compassionate servant. **Relationship with father unchanged**: Rawdon affectionate and devoted; maintains private interviews mornings during shaving; sweetmeats hidden in old epaulet box. Father buys picture-books; walls covered with pictures. Takes accustomed morning walks with father and pony. **Chapter 18 plan**: Rebecca forbids him traveling to Queen's Crawley; instructs Rawdon that boy too big to travel "bodkin" between them; let him stay in nursery; Briggs can make black frock.

**Miss Briggs (Chapter 19)**
- **Background**: Miss Crawley's faithful retainer for score of years; received little annuity from Miss Crawley's legacy. **Dismissal (Chapter 19)**: Lady Southdown dismissed her as quickly as decency permitted; Mr. Pitt made no objection. **Post-dismissal and reunion (Chapter 19)**: Fatigued from weary walk to Times Office in City inserting advertisement for sixth time; reached Mr. Bowls's door where she lodged. Rebecca recognizes her, pulls up carriage, embraces warmly. They retire to Mrs. Bowls's front parlour; Briggs cried; Becky laughed and kissed her. Briggs told all her history amidst sobs and wonder; Rebecca gave narrative of own life with artlessness and candour. **Mrs. Bowls's warning**: Cautioned Briggs against venturing into "lion's den," warning "you will rue it, Miss B., mark my words, and as sure as my name is Bowls." Briggs promised to be cautious. **Outcome**: Briggs went to live with Mrs. Rawdon next week; within six months lent Rawdon Crawley six hundred pounds upon annuity.

**Mrs. Bute Crawley – Schemer (Chapter 18)**
- **Character**: Considers herself one of most virtuous women in England. Daughters: Martha, Emma, Fanny, Matilda. **Reality**: Nobody sees poor girls; Mamma drilling them hour after hour. Got over yachting men, parsons, officers; tried to inveigle barristers. **Upon Sir Pitt's illness and death (Chapter 18)**: Immediately summoned; assumes command; watches through night; never seems to want sleep. Calls Horrocks "tipsy old wretch"; bids him never show face again or be transported. Seizes candle; orders room search; orchestrates household. **Post-death**: Dismissed Briggs as quickly as decency permitted; exercises dowager's authority without Mr. Pitt's objection.

**Bowls and Firkin (Chapter 19)**
- Received legacies from Miss Crawley; married and set up lodging-house in London. Mrs. Bowls (late Firkin) cautions Briggs against Rebecca, remarking she wouldn't trust Rawdon; does not like account of Colonel's menage from Raggles. Salutes Rebecca with sour curtsey when she leaves parlour; fingers like "so many sausages, cold and lifeless" when holding them out in deference, though Rebecca persists in shaking hands.

**Lady Jane Crawley (now Lady Pitt) (Chapter 19)**
- **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: In black, ready to receive Rawdon and Rebecca. Takes both hands of sister-in-law and kisses her affectionately. Embrace brought tears to Rebecca's eyes; artless mark of kindness and confidence touched and pleased her. Blushes exceedingly when Rawdon salutes her with kiss. Called "dev'lish nice little woman" by Rawdon. Good to everybody including Briggs.

**Other Characters Status Unchanged**: Colonel Dobbin, Amelia Osborne, Georgy, Lord Steyne, Reverend Bute Crawley, James Crawley, Miss Horrocks (now married to saddler at Mudbury), Hester (maid), Horrocks (butler).

## Critical Facts
- **Sir Pitt dies summer 1816**: Collapses after heavy drinking; becomes helpless; dies after days of decline.
- **Pitt becomes Sir Pitt, Baronet and MP**: Within days determines to rule justly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations.
- **Briggs dismissed but connected**: Released by Lady Southdown; reconnects with Rebecca who invites her to live with them; lends Rawdon six hundred pounds within six months.
- **Funeral at Queen's Crawley (Autumn 1816)**: Rawdon and Rebecca return; Pitt has gotten fat; Lady Jane warmly greets Rebecca, bringing tears; Lady Southdown maintains cold silence; sisters summoned from school; elaborate mourning ceremony with many townspeople assembled in black.
- **Rebecca's nature revealed**: Still manipulates Briggs (securing six hundred pounds loan); feigns tender interest in sisters-in-law's education; pretends not to be impostor; enjoys social recognition; capable of genuine emotional response (tears from Lady Jane's kindness).
